Each person has a unique value for each attribute (so each attribute's values are assigned uniquely to the two persons: i.e., one person has cooking, the other chess; one person engineer, the other chef; one person thai, the other canadian). So each attribute is a permutation of the two values across the two persons.

Given constraints:

1) "The person who is a engineer is not anywhere to the left of the person who likes chess". Means the engineer is not left of the chess person. So either engineer is to the right of chess person (i.e., engineer position > chess position) OR they could be in same position? No, they are distinct persons, so engineer cannot be left of chess. So engineer must be either same position? Not possible because each person has unique job; chess is a hobby, not a job; engineer and chess are attributes of different persons. So engineer is not left of chess => engineer position >= chess position? Actually "not anywhere to the left of" means there is no position where engineer is left of chess. So engineer cannot be left; can be right or same? Same position impossible because they are different persons. So engineer must be to the right of the chess person. So engineer position > chess position.

Thus: position(engineer) > position(chess).

2) "The person who likes cooking is somewhere to the left of the person who is thai". Means cooking person is left of thai person. So position(cook) < position(thai).

- Hobby of P1: H1 ∈ {cooking, chess}
- Hobby of P2: H2 = the other.

- Job of P1: J1 ∈ {engineer, chef}

- Nationality of P1: N1 ∈ {thai, canadian}

Constraints:

C1: position(engineer) > position(chess). So engineer is to the right of chess person.

Constraint: Epos > ChessPos.

C2: position(cook) < position(thai). Let CookPos = position of person whose hobby is cooking. ThaiPos = position of person whose nationality is thai.
